title: Renovascular Hypertension Workup
subtitle: When to suspect RAS and intervene

steps.title: Clinical clues
steps.body: Resistant hypertension, flash pulmonary edema, asymmetric kidney size, new AKI after ACEi/ARB, or abdominal bruit in at-risk patients (atherosclerosis, fibromuscular dysplasia).
steps.tip: Bilateral RAS is a contraindication to ACEi/ARB — think before starting.

steps.title: Screening imaging
steps.body: Duplex ultrasound is first-line in many centers. CTA or MRA for anatomic detail. Digital subtraction angiography remains gold standard before intervention.
steps.tip: CTA may overestimate stenosis; correlate with clinical context.

steps.title: When to revascularize
steps.body: Significant stenosis with recurrent flash edema, resistant HTN despite ≥3 drugs, or progressive CKD attributable to ischemic nephropathy.
steps.tip: Medical therapy alone is reasonable in stable atherosclerotic RAS without compelling indications.

steps.title: Post-procedure monitoring
steps.body: Watch for contrast nephropathy, restenosis, and AKI after stenting. Recheck creatinine and BP within 1–2 weeks.
steps.tip: FMD in young women often responds well to angioplasty without stent.
